client: I've been really struggling since I got promoted last month. I keep second-guessing every decision I make at work, and I'm constantly worried I'm going to mess something up. Part of me feels like I don't deserve this position, and that they made a mistake choosing me.
therapist: I hear both worry and urgency in your voice as you share this—it sounds like this promotion has really shaken your confidence. Would it help to explore what evidence there is that you *do* belong in this role, versus the fears that you don’t?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, loud, fast speech

client: I know logically that I must have done something right to get promoted, but it's hard to focus on that when I'm constantly catching small mistakes in my work. I keep thinking if I were truly qualified, these things wouldn't slip through so easily.
therapist: I notice your voice sounds hesitant and quieter than usual—it seems that self-doubt is really weighing on you right now. Could we examine whether these "small mistakes" might actually be normal parts of learning any new role, rather than proof you don’t belong?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, moderate-paced speech

client: I guess everyone makes mistakes when they're new... but it feels different for me. When my coworkers make errors, they just laugh it off, but I obsess over mine for days. I can't shake the feeling that I'm being held to a higher standard now that I'm in this position.
therapist: Your voice sounds really strained—this pressure you're putting on yourself seems both intense and exhausting. Let's challenge that assumption about higher standards—what would it look like if you gave yourself the same grace your coworkers do?

client: I don't know if I could ever be that relaxed about mistakes. What if giving myself grace just makes me complacent? I've always pushed myself hard - that's how I got promoted in the first place. If I ease up now, won't I just start slipping?
therapist: Your voice sounds tight with worry—this fear of slipping seems to be holding you in a really difficult bind. Could we explore whether there might be a middle ground between complacency and constant self-punishment, where healthy standards actually help you grow in this role?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, moderate-paced speech

client: I've never really thought about a middle ground before - it's always been all or nothing for me. The idea of being less harsh with myself makes me anxious though. How do I know where to draw the line between being appropriately careful and being too hard on myself?
therapist: I hear the nervousness in your softer voice—this concept of balance feels unfamiliar and unsettling to you. Let's start small: what's one situation where you could experiment with being *slightly* gentler with yourself, just to observe what happens?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, moderate-paced speech

client: Maybe I could try not beating myself up when I send an email with a typo? That happens sometimes and I usually replay it in my head for hours. But it's scary to think if I stop being hard on myself about the small things, I'll start missing bigger mistakes too.
therapist: Your voice sounds small and tentative—this first step feels scary but important. What if we look at this experiment not as "letting mistakes slide," but as redirecting that same energy you put into self-criticism toward constructive learning instead?

client: Redirecting the energy sounds better than just letting go completely, but how do I actually do that? When I catch a mistake, my first instinct is always to panic. It's hard to switch that immediate reaction to something more constructive.
therapist: I hear both curiosity and nervous energy in your voice—you're genuinely wanting to try this new approach, but that automatic panic is still so strong. vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, moderate-paced speech

client: Maybe I could try taking three deep breaths when I notice a mistake, before I react? That seems simple enough. But I'm worried that in the moment, I'll be too caught up in the panic to remember to do it. These reactions feel so automatic.
therapist: Your voice sounds hesitant yet hopeful—it's clear you're trying to find a way through this while still feeling understandably nervous about old patterns kicking in. client: I could try putting a sticky note on my monitor, but I worry my coworkers will see it and think I'm incompetent. Maybe a phone reminder would be more discreet, but then I might ignore it when I'm in the middle of panicking about a mistake. It feels like there's no perfect solution.
therapist: Your voice sounds rushed and higher than usual—I can hear how much this dilemma is stirring up anxiety for you.
